text: Four-hundred-thousand men marched into Russia. Barely ten-thousand came back.
June eighteen-twelve. The biggest army Europe had ever seen crossed a river on the edge of the Russian Empire.
Six months later, the survivors stumbled back across the same river. Ragged, frozen, a few hundred at a time.
So here is today's question. Where did Europe's greatest army go? And no, it wasn't just the winter.
Let's follow it on the map.
First, the man. In seventeen-ninety-three, a twenty-four-year-old artillery officer named Napoleon Bonaparte helped take the port of Toulon back from the British.
Six years later he seized power in Paris. In eighteen-oh-four, he crowned himself Emperor of the French.
Then he beat almost everyone. Austria at Austerlitz. Prussia at Jena. Russia at Friedland.
By eighteen-ten, France ruled from Spain to the Baltic, and most of the rest of Europe was its ally or its puppet.
Quick quiz. Which of these did Napoleon never conquer? Austria, Prussia, or Britain?
Britain. Behind the Royal Navy, it was the one enemy he could not reach. And that is how Russia gets dragged into this story.
In eighteen-oh-six, Napoleon tried to beat Britain with money instead of guns. He banned all of Europe from trading with it.
In eighteen-oh-seven, after his defeat at Friedland, Tsar Alexander the First made peace on a raft in the middle of a river, and agreed to join the ban.
But Russia lived on selling grain, timber and hemp to Britain. The ban was strangling its economy.
On the last day of eighteen-ten, Alexander opened his ports to neutral ships and slapped taxes on French goods. In practice, he had walked out.
And then there was Poland. Napoleon had built a Polish state right on Russia's border. The Tsar saw a knife at his throat.
So Napoleon made his decision. March into Russia, win one big battle, and force the Tsar back into line. A short war.
To do it, he gathered the largest army Europe had ever assembled. The Grande Armée.
About four-hundred-fifty-thousand men in the first wave. Around six-hundred-thousand in all, once the reinforcements came up.
Only about half of them were French. Poles, Germans, Italians, Austrians, Prussians, Swiss. A whole continent in one army.
The Poles alone sent close to one-hundred-thousand men. They hoped Napoleon would give them back their country.
It took up to two-hundred-thousand horses and about one-thousand-three-hundred cannon.
The problem was food. An army this size eats a mountain every day, and Russia's roads were dirt tracks.
Napoleon brought supplies for a few weeks. He was sure the war would be over by then.
On the twenty-fourth of June eighteen-twelve, the army crossed the Neman river at Kovno, today's Kaunas in Lithuania.
Now watch this line. Its width is the number of men. This is how a French engineer, Charles Minard, drew this campaign in eighteen-sixty-nine.
Napoleon wanted a battle. The Russians refused to give him one. Their two armies kept pulling back, deeper and deeper.
Four days after crossing, he took Vilna without a fight. The Russians had already left.
As they went, they burned crops, villages, and anything the French could eat.
Then came the weather. Summer storms that turned roads to mud, then scorching heat, dust, and bad water.
Typhus and dysentery spread through the ranks. Horses died by the thousands in the first weeks.
Men deserted, fell behind, or simply dropped. In the first month alone, about one-hundred-thousand were gone.
At Vitebsk, in late July, Napoleon stopped for two weeks, hoping the Russians would finally come and fight. They never did.
Look at the line. It's already a third thinner, and the real fighting hasn't even started.
In mid-August, at Smolensk, the French finally caught the Russians. The city burned, and the Russians slipped away again.
In three days of fighting, around ten-thousand French and twelve-thousand Russians were killed or wounded.
Napoleon had a choice. Stop for the winter, or push on to Moscow. He pushed on.
In Russia, people were furious about the endless retreat. The Tsar gave command to an old, one-eyed general. Mikhail Kutuzov.
And Kutuzov finally turned to fight. At a village called Borodino, about one-hundred-twenty kilometres west of Moscow.

The seventh of September eighteen-twelve. About one-hundred-thirty-thousand French and allies, against more than one-hundred-twenty-thousand Russians, and over one-thousand-two-hundred cannon between them.
They fought from dawn until dark, over Russian earthworks: the flèches, and the Great Redoubt.
By nightfall, more than seventy-thousand men were dead or wounded. The bloodiest single day of the Napoleonic Wars.
Napoleon refused to send in his Imperial Guard, his last reserve. The Russian army survived, and pulled back in order.
The French held the field. But it was not the knockout blow Napoleon needed.
Quiz time. After Borodino, what did Kutuzov do? Attack again, defend Moscow, or give Moscow up?
He gave it up. Without a fight. To save its army, Russia abandoned its ancient capital.
On the fourteenth of September, Napoleon reached Moscow. He waited for the city's leaders to bring him the keys. Nobody came.
Of a city of two-hundred-seventy-thousand people, almost everyone had left.
That night, fires broke out. For four days Moscow burned. About three quarters of the city was destroyed.
Who started it? Most historians blame the Russians themselves, probably on the orders of the governor, Rostopchin. It's still debated.
Napoleon sat in the Kremlin and wrote to the Tsar, offering peace. Alexander never answered.
For five weeks the Emperor waited in a burned city, as autumn turned cold. His army looted, drank, and fell apart.
On the eighteenth of October, Kutuzov struck a French outpost south of Moscow, at Tarutino. Napoleon finally understood. There would be no peace.
On the nineteenth of October, he finally ordered the retreat. About one-hundred-thousand men marched out, dragging carts full of loot.
Behind them, on Napoleon's orders, the rearguard blew up parts of the Kremlin.
He tried to go home by a new road, south, through untouched farmland. At Maloyaroslavets, the Russians blocked the way.
So the army turned back onto the road it came in on. The road it had already stripped bare.
At Vyazma, on the third of November, Russian troops caught the rearguard and mauled it. The retreat became a running fight.
In early November, real winter arrived. On Minard's map, a second line appears at the bottom. The temperature.
The last horses died. Cannon and wagons were left in the snow. Without cavalry, nobody could scout or guard the column.
Cossacks rode out of the forests, cut down stragglers, and vanished. Anyone who fell behind was lost.
Men burned wagons for warmth and ate the horses that fell. By early December, nights dropped below minus thirty degrees.
On the ninth of November, the army staggered back into Smolensk. Only about sixty-thousand men were still fit to fight.
At Krasnoi, in mid-November, the Russians struck again. Marshal Ney's rearguard was almost wiped out.
Then came the Berezina river. The bridge had been burned, and Russian armies were closing in from three sides.
French engineers under General Eblé stood in the freezing water for hours and built two bridges. Few of them lived to see the spring.
For three days the army crossed. On the last morning the bridges were burned, and thousands of stragglers were left on the far bank.
On the fifth of December, Napoleon left his army and raced back to Paris in a sledge.
In mid-December, the last of the main army crossed the Neman again. On Minard's map, a band of four-hundred-twenty-two-thousand men ends at ten-thousand.
Counting the corps on the flanks, maybe one-hundred-thousand got out in all. But the Grande Armée was gone.
So, where did Europe's greatest army go?
Mostly not to the winter. Look at the line. Most of it had already vanished before the first snow fell.
It was distance. Supply. Disease. Heat. A Russian army that refused to fight on Napoleon's terms, and a country willing to burn its own land.
Russia paid a terrible price too. Hundreds of thousands of soldiers and civilians died.
On the French side, around one-hundred-thousand men were taken prisoner.
Within weeks, his allies began to turn. On the thirtieth of December, the Prussian corps in his army made its own deal with the Russians.
In October eighteen-thirteen, at Leipzig, more than half a million soldiers met in the largest battle of the Napoleonic Wars. Napoleon lost.
For Napoleon, it was the beginning of the end. In less than two years, his enemies were in Paris, and he was in exile on Elba.
And the best picture of this disaster was drawn fifty-seven years later, by a retired French engineer. Some call it the best statistical graphic ever made.
Now, your turn. If you were Napoleon, when would you have turned back? Tell me in the comments.
